contract.basis: Every field in this catalogue is declared with a concrete type and no null union — courtCentre.name/roomName, prosecutionCaseIdentifier.{majorCreditorCode,caseURN,prosecutionAuthorityReference,prosecutionAuthorityName,prosecutionAuthorityOUCode}, person.{middleName,nationalityCode} and offence.{offenceTitle} are "type":"string"; prosecutionCase.isGroupMaster and defendant.isYouth are "type":"boolean"; the rest are $refs to object or integer schemas (address, plea, verdict, courtOrder, personTitle, custodyEstablishment, positiveInteger, uuid). Verified against cpp-platform-core-domain/criminal-court-public-model/src/main/resources/json/schema/global/. In this model "optional" means ABSENT, never present-with-null, so a null here is a contract violation and not a producible input.
contract.note: The producer cannot emit this. The recording is what the Node app DOES with the input, and is evidence about robustness; it is NOT a parity obligation. provenance.operatorDescription: Sets one optional field to JSON null (the key is present, the value is null).
provenance.operatorRationale: EVERY variant of this operator is SCHEMA_INVALID and is recorded as such: the model types these fields concretely with no null union, so "optional" means absent, never present-with-null. The operator is kept because the recordings are the evidence for what the Node app does with a null — it does not guard against one, and copies it straight into the outbound body, producing 18 documents that violate the frozen add-informant-register contract (README.md §5 finding 6). That is a robustness observation and a decision to take with Results; it is NOT a parity obligation on the Java port. Absent and null are different inputs and JavaScript treats them almost — but not exactly — alike (`x && x.y` is falsy for both; `Object.keys` and `hasOwnProperty` are not), which is how the null survives to the wire.
